doc.title: Stanley Kay interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clearwater Beach, Florida, March 18, 2001

title: His role as Buddy Rich's assistant drummer and other employers
summary: Kay corrects the myth that he drove the bus or played the charts; he played acts and vocals, later worked with Frankie Laine, Patti Page and Josephine Baker.

story.theme_name: Medicine shows, minstrels, circuses and the black theater circuit
story.community_name: On the road with minstrel, carnival and tent shows

blocks.x: Yeah. How did it work with being in with Buddy Rich. He played part of the time?

No. What it was, see it’s a fallacy. People write what they think. They think that I drove the bus, which I never did because I couldn’t ride a bicycle. I didn’t drive any bus. I could drive a car. What it was is I was his assistant so to speak. In other words they said that I went and played the charts and he sat when we got a new chart, that he sat in front listening to me play. That’s not true. Because when he was with Tommy, Harry James, Artie Shaw, there was no assistant drummer. He could play it the first time he heard it. So all I did was if he wanted to sing, I played. And when we did a dance if he felt like doing that, he did it. When we played the Paramount Theater or the Strand or all those theaters we played all over, the Apollo and the Howard in Washington and the Regal in Chicago, I played the acts when he wanted me to do it. But then it was interesting because playing with your idol, like if he would compliment me, if he would say, “boy you really sounded good,” I didn’t want to hear that because I didn’t believe it. See? So I’d say, “oh the bus is leaving at four o’clock.” I didn’t want to hear I play good. I don’t want to hear that. Because you know, you’re playing with your idol. It was better for me when I joined like Frankie Laine for six years and Patti Page and Josephine Baker. But we toured with Josephine. It was Sweets Edison, Buddy and myself. And Sherrie [Maricle] will tell you, with the band, that sometimes — she’s a fabulous drummer and a great leader and a brilliant musician, far better than I ever was, she’s far better than I ever was, really, that’s truthful. She’s a musician. She’s a composer, she’s a doctor of music you know. But they kid me. She said, “well you know our manager and our founder Stanley Kay he

contributed a lot to jazz.” And everybody in the audience in listening. They’ve got their ears up. And they says, “you don’t know this, but he was the original drummer of ‘How Much is that Doggie in the Window’ with Patti Page.” And I was.
